428.title: Bhakti — the first use of the word in the Upanishads (6.23)
428.hook: the very last verse of the Shvetashvatara uses a word that will one day fill India's temples with song
428.carry: to one who has the highest devotion
428.tomorrow: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit
428.howItsDone: Bhakti is lived across Hindu traditions through kirtan and bhajan singing, temple worship, repeating God's name, and honoring one's teacher, and many devotees treat love of God as the heart of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anor aniyan, smaller than small, greater than great, hidden in the heart and past the stars. The paradox.

On a festival night at a Hindu temple, the sound can reach the street before you reach the door: bells, drums, a crowd singing one name over and over, someone in tears at the front. That whole world of love poured toward God has a name, bhakti, devotion. You met it in year one with Mirabai and the saints. But where does the word first show up in these old texts? You have to read to the very end of the Shvetashvatara, to its final verse.
screen: `BELLS, DRUMS, ONE NAME SUNG.` → `THE WORLD OF BHAKTI.` → `WHERE DOES THE WORD BEGIN?`

segments.voice: Verse 6.23, in paraphrase: for the great soul who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the teacher as to God, these things that have been taught shine out. They truly shine out for that great soul. Highest devotion is para bhakti. Bhakti comes from a root, bhaj, that means to share, to take part, to belong. Some teachers draw on that root: devotion as belonging, a share in God, and not only a feeling. Scholars often point to this verse as the first time the word bhakti appears in the principal Upanishads in this sense, devotion to a personal God. It's a striking place to find it. This Upanishad has spent six chapters on the wheel, the swan, the fire sticks, the posture, Rudra the one Lord, the self smaller than small. Its last verse doesn't add more knowledge. It names devotion: the teaching shines, the verse says, for the one who loves. Notice the teacher, too. Devotion to the guru as to God is part of the same verse, and many Hindu traditions honor the teacher this way. Not everyone reads it alike: Advaita teachers often treat devotion as what readies the mind for knowledge, while devotional schools treat it as the goal itself. Later in this course, the Bhagavad Gita makes this word a whole path.
screen: `PARA BHAKTI: THE HIGHEST DEVOTION.` · `BHAJ: TO SHARE, TO BELONG.` · `THE LAST VERSE IS ABOUT LOVE.` · then, large: `IT SHINES FOR THE ONE WHO LOVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you love without needing anything back: a person, a teacher, a place, or, if you pray, God as you know God. Let that feeling sit in your chest without pushing it bigger, and notice what it does to the shoulders, the breath, the face. Then see whether anything you think about looks different while that love is present.
Bhakti. Devotion, from a root that means to share or to belong. Its first appearance in the principal Upanishads is in the Shvetashvatara's last verse.
Your line: to one who has the highest devotion. Tomorrow, the seven Upanishads in one sit. See you then.

429.title: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit
429.hook: fourteen weeks, seven Upanishads, one sit to hold them all, and the three words that tie them together
429.tomorrow: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind
429.howItsDone: Hindu traditions treat these Upanishads as the heart of the Vedanta: students chant and study them with a teacher, and the great sayings, such as tat tvam asi and prajnanam brahma, are taught as summaries of the whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, the Shvetashvatara's last word. The teaching shines for one with the highest devotion. Today, the last day of the Upanishads.

Ninety-seven days ago you started with one syllable, om, chanted at a Vedic sacrifice. Since then: dogs chanting for breakfast, a boy telling the truth at a teacher's door, a woman who asked what water is woven on, a man whose head fell off for asking too much, two birds on a tree, a wheel, a swan, a pair of fire sticks. Seven books. Fourteen weeks. Today, before moving on, all seven in one sit, and the line that runs through every one.

The Chandogya came first. Uddalaka hands his son salt dissolved in water: taste it here, here, everywhere. That essence is the self of all. Tat tvam asi: you are that. The Brihadaranyaka. Yajnavalkya won't let anyone pin the self down: not this, not this. And Maitreyi asks the question that matters: what would I do with wealth that can't make me immortal? The Taittiriya: five sheaths, from food to breath to mind to understanding, and at the very center, bliss. The Aitareya: the self enters the body through the crown of the head, and near the end comes a great saying, consciousness is Brahman. The Prashna: six students wait a year to ask their questions, and every answer comes back to breath and om. The Mundaka: two kinds of knowledge, a bow and an arrow, two birds, and rivers losing their names in the sea. The Shvetashvatara: the wheel, the swan, the one Lord, and the highest devotion. Seven voices, centuries apart, read differently by different schools. Advaita teachers hear in them one reality without a second. Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers hear a self that belongs to God and is never simply erased. All of them treasure the same verses. And the thread they pull on is Uddalaka's: what you're looking for is not far away. Tat tvam asi.

segments.voice: Sit in the posture from four days ago and take seven breaths, one for each book: salt everywhere; not this, not this; inward, sheath by sheath, to joy; consciousness is Brahman; the breath itself; the river reaching the sea; devotion, in whatever form is yours. Then let the rest of the sit be quiet, with three words underneath it: you are that.

Uddalaka, the sage who taught his son with salt dissolved in water. Ninety-eight sessions in seven of the principal Upanishads, from om at the Chandogya's opening to bhakti in the Shvetashvatara's last verse, carry his thread.
Your line: tat tvam asi, you are that. Tomorrow, a new text begins, the Yoga Sutras. Block A, done.

430.title: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind (1.1–1.2)
430.hook: the most famous text on yoga opens with a single small word, and defines yoga in four more
430.tomorrow: then the seer rests in itself
430.howItsDone: Students of yoga in many Hindu lineages begin study of the Yoga Sutras by chanting 1.1 and 1.2, often with Vyasa's classic commentary, and treat 1.2 as the definition the whole text unfolds.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Upanishads closed with Uddalaka's three words: tat tvam asi, you are that. Today a new block begins: the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali.

A yoga studio: mats, mirrors, someone holding a long, shaking plank. The book behind the word looks nothing like that. The Yoga Sutras are short threads of Sanskrit, gathered under the name Patanjali, and only three of those threads deal with posture. The rest are about the mind. And the book opens with a word so small you could miss it. One word, then a definition commentators have been unpacking ever since.
screen: `MATS, MIRRORS, A SHAKING PLANK.` → `SHORT THREADS OF SANSKRIT.` → `THREE ABOUT POSTURE. THE REST: THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.1: atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha means now, and in old Sanskrit books it marks a beginning: here the real subject starts. A traditional verse says two sounds came first from the creator's throat, om and atha, so both are lucky words to begin with. Some teachers also hear a quieter meaning: now, when you are ready, after everything else has been tried. Anushasanam is interesting too. Commentators read its anu, after, as a teaching that comes after: handed down, not invented on the spot. Then sutra 1.2 gives the whole definition: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta is the mind, the whole field of thinking and feeling. Vritti is a turning, a whirl, the way water turns in an eddy. Nirodha means stopping, or holding still. So yoga, in this book, isn't a shape you make with the body. It's the moment the mind's whirling settles. No god is named yet, no stretch, no secret. Just the mind, its movements, and the possibility that they can quiet down. The rest of the first chapter is a manual for that. The Upanishads spoke of what you are. Patanjali's book, from a different school with its own map, starts with a practical question: what is the mind doing, and how does it settle, starting now?
screen: `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `ANUSHASANAM: HANDED DOWN.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and watch the turnings: a thought arrives, swirls, goes. Each time you notice you've been carried off, say one word silently, now, atha, not as a scolding but as a fresh start, and settle back on the breath. Every return is the first sutra, said again.
"Now. The first word of the Yoga Sutras, atha: the teaching begins here, and so does the practice, every time you come back.
Your line: atha, now. A fresh start, never a correction. That's day four hundred thirty.

431.title: Then the seer rests in itself (1.3–1.4)
431.hook: when the mind's whirling settles, what's left? Patanjali's answer is the one who was watching all along
431.howItsDone: In Patanjali's yoga, practitioners learn to witness the mind's movements rather than become them, and many Hindu teachers describe meditation as resting as the witness, sakshi, behind thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atha, now. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. So when the turnings go still, what's left?

You're at a movie, completely absorbed. You flinch at the jump scare. You tear up at the ending. For two hours you are the story. Then the lights come up, and there you are, in a sticky seat, popcorn on your shirt, and you realize: I was here the whole time. The story was on the screen. I was the one watching. Patanjali's next two sutras are about that moment when the lights come up.
screen: `TWO HOURS INSIDE THE STORY.` → `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `I WAS WATCHING ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.3: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then the seer rests in its own form. Tada, then: once the turnings are stilled. Drashtri, the seer: in Patanjali's system, pure awareness, which he also calls purusha. Svarupa, its own form, its true nature. Avasthana, abiding, staying put. So when the whirling stops, nothing is lost. The seer is simply left as it always was. Sutra 1.4 covers the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer seems to take on the form of the turnings. That's the movie. Anger rises in the mind, and awareness seems to become anger. A worry spins, and awareness seems to be the worry. The word seems matters. In this system the seer never actually changes. It only looks that way, the way the moon looks broken on rippled water. Teachers often use that picture: still the ripples and the reflection is whole again, though the moon itself was never in pieces. Here Patanjali leans on an older school, Samkhya, which separates purusha, pure awareness, from prakriti, everything that changes, including the mind. The mind is not the seer. It's the screen. Vedanta schools describe the seer and the world in their own terms, and the Yoga Sutras keep theirs. But on this point they meet: the one who sees is not the passing thoughts it sees.

Then lean your attention slightly back toward the one who is noticing, without trying to find or describe it, the way you settle into your seat when the lights come up.

432.title: The five turnings — right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep, memory (1.5–1.11)
432.hook: Patanjali sorts everything your mind does into five kinds, and two of them will surprise you
432.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five vrittis as a map for meditation, labeling movements of the mind so they can be noticed and released rather than followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: drashtri, the seer, the one who watches the movie and is never changed by it.

Ten minutes of an ordinary mind might go like this. Read something and understand it. Misjudge someone's tone in a text. Rehearse a conversation that hasn't happened. Remember the call to an aunt that never got made. Nod off for a second. It feels like a thousand different things. Patanjali says it's five. Every turning of the mind is one of five kinds, and sutra 1.5 adds a twist first: each kind can be painful or not painful.
screen: `TEN MINUTES OF A MIND.` → `A THOUSAND THINGS? NO: FIVE.` → `PAINFUL, OR NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, sutras 1.6 to 1.11. One: pramana, right knowledge. It comes three ways: perception, inference, and reliable testimony, like trusting a good teacher or a scripture. Two: viparyaya, error, a picture that doesn't match the real form. The classic example is a coiled rope in the dusk taken for a snake. Three: vikalpa, often translated imagination, or verbal delusion: knowledge that follows words with nothing real behind them. Indian logicians liked the example of a hare's horn: you can say it, almost picture it, and it isn't there. Some teachers say a lot of worry lives here. Four: nidra, sleep. The first surprise: Patanjali counts dreamless sleep as a turning too, one that rests on absence. The commentator Vyasa notes that you wake and say, I slept well, so something was registering. Five: smriti, memory, holding on to what you've already experienced. The second surprise: right knowledge is on the list. Even true thoughts are turnings. Yoga is the stilling of all of them, not just the wrong ones. Why sort them? Teachers say a turning you can name tends to loosen its grip. That snake in the dark is just a rope. That argument in your head is just vikalpa, words without an object.

segments.voice: Be a gentle sorter: when a thought arises, give it one of five silent labels. Knowing, a car outside; error, that voice was the fridge; imagining, a conversation that isn't happening; sleep, a drifting fog; memory, something from yesterday. Don't argue with any of them; label, let it pass, and come back to the breath.
Vritti, a turning, a whirl of the mind. Patanjali names five kinds: right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep and memory, the movements yoga learns to still.
Your line: five. Five turnings, all counted on one hand, even the true ones. See you tomorrow.

433.title: Practice and non-attachment (1.12–1.16)
433.hook: how do you still the turnings? Patanjali gives two tools, and they pull in opposite directions
433.howItsDone: Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages describe abhyasa and vairagya as the two wings of spiritual life, practiced through daily meditation or prayer kept up over years and a steady loosening of craving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vritti, the five turnings of the mind: knowing, error, imagining, sleep and memory.

Learning to ride a bike takes two things at once. Keep pedaling, keep showing up. And stop gripping the handlebars so hard that every wobble becomes a crash. Effort and letting go. Too much of one and the bike never moves; too much of the other and it tips over. Sutra 1.12 is only a few words long, and it says the turnings of the mind are stilled by a pair like that.
screen: `KEEP PEDALING.` → `LOOSEN THE GRIP.` → `EFFORT AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.12: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. They are stilled by practice and non-attachment. Abhyasa, practice, is defined in 1.13 as the effort to stay steady in that stillness. Then 1.14 adds the fine print: practice becomes firmly rooted when it's done for a long time, without breaks, and with devotion, or real care. Long, unbroken, wholehearted. No shortcut is offered. Vairagya, non-attachment, comes in 1.15: the mastery of someone who no longer thirsts for things, whether things seen or things only heard about. That second category is interesting. The commentators take it to include rewards promised in scripture, even heaven. So non-attachment isn't only letting go of dessert. It's letting go of spiritual prizes too. And 1.16 names a higher non-attachment still: when, from knowing the seer, one no longer thirsts even for the three strands of nature themselves. The two tools balance. Practice is the gas. Non-attachment is easing off a brake you might not know you're pressing. Practice without letting go becomes grim and grabby; letting go without practice becomes drift. Patanjali isn't alone in pairing them. In the Bhagavad Gita, when Arjuna complains that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, Krishna gives the same two words: by practice and by detachment it can be held.
screen: `ABHYASA: THE EFFORT TO STAY STEADY.` · `LONG, UNBROKEN, WHOLEHEARTED.` · `VAIRAGYA: NO MORE THIRST.` · then, large: `THE GITA PAIRS THEM TOO.`

segments.voice: For the first half of this sit, practice: return to the breath, gently, every time you drift. For the second half, keep returning, but let go of wanting the sit to go well, wanting calm, wanting insight. Just return, and want nothing from returning.
Nirodha, stilling. Abhyasa and vairagya, practice and non-attachment, are what still the mind's turnings: the steady effort to return, and the letting go of thirst.
Your line: abhyasa, vairagya. The gas, and the loosened brake. Day four hundred thirty-three, done.

434.title: Samadhi with seed (1.17–1.18)
434.hook: Patanjali's deepest absorption comes in two kinds: one that still rests on something, and one that rests on nothing
434.tomorrow: the born-free and the rest of us
434.howItsDone: Teachers of classical yoga describe samadhi in stages, first with an object of meditation and then beyond any object, and students usually work for years with a single support, such as the breath, a mantra or a divine form.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirodha, stilled by abhyasa and vairagya, the gas and the loosened brake. Today closes a week that crossed from one book into another.

A camera zooms in. First a whole hillside. Then one tree. Then one leaf, so close you can see its veins. Then just the light falling on the leaf. Then, strangest of all, the camera turns around and looks at the one holding it. Each step narrower and finer than the last. Patanjali describes the mind's absorption a bit like that zoom. And in the very next sutra, he describes what happens when there's nothing left in the frame at all.
screen: `THE HILLSIDE, THE TREE, THE LEAF.` → `JUST THE LIGHT.` → `THEN: NOTHING IN THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: Samadhi means absorption: the mind so gathered on something that the scattering stops. Sutra 1.17 describes the first kind, samprajnata, absorption with awareness of an object, in four stages from coarse to fine. Vitarka: absorbed in something gross, like a physical object. Vichara: in something subtle. Ananda: in joy. Asmita: in the bare sense of I am. Hillside, leaf, light, the one holding the camera. In every stage there's still something the mind rests on, a support. Later in the chapter Patanjali names this kind samadhi with seed, sabija. Sutra 1.18 describes the other kind. It comes from practicing the letting go of every support, and what remains are only faint traces, the samskaras, impressions left in the mind. No object at all. The seed is what the mind still holds, and anything held can sprout again. Now the week. Day one, bhakti, the highest devotion. Day two, the seven Upanishads closed with tat tvam asi. Day three, a new book opened with one word, atha, now. Day four, the seer rests in itself. Day five, the five turnings. Day six, practice and non-attachment. And today, with and without: the mind resting on something, and the mind resting on nothing.
screen: `SAMADHI: THE MIND GATHERED.` · `FOUR STAGES, COARSE TO FINE.` · `1.18: NO SUPPORT LEFT.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `WITH SEED, WITHOUT SEED.`

segments.voice: Do the zoom gently: rest first on the whole body sitting, then just the breath at the nostrils, then any ease that's there, then the plain feeling of being here, I am. Stay there. If even that thins out for a moment, let it, without chasing it or holding on.
Sabija, with seed. Samadhi that still rests on a support, coarse or subtle, joy or the bare sense of I am, as opposed to absorption with no seed at all.
Your line: with, without. The mind resting on something, or on nothing. Week sixty-two, done.
